domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is agent loops, the workflow-to-agent spectrum, multi-agent architectures, ambient agents, and human-in-the-loop control patterns, which are core harness and control-plane concerns. The framing is enterprise agent deployment (enterprise_operations), built on LangGraph/LangChain as developer tooling (developer_platforms), with repeated coding-agent examples like Replit and Claude Code (coding_assistants). The talk explicitly addresses moving agents from prototype to production and designing agent architectures for reliable enterprise deployment. The content covers practical frameworks and patterns for practitioners without requiring deep mathematical or implementation-level detail. This is a recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Multiple evidence anchors are directly cited from the transcript with said_in_transcript grade, supporting the classification claims.

summary: Harrison Chase presents three ingredients for building reliable enterprise agents, grounded in a first-principles framework credited to conversations with Assaf (head of AI at Monday, GPT researcher author). The core equation: (probability of success × value when right) minus (cost when wrong) must exceed the cost of running the agent. To increase value, Chase recommends targeting high-value verticals—citing Harvey in legal and research/summarization in finance—and shifting interaction patterns from quick Q&A or co-pilot responses toward long-running, autonomous agents such as deep research and ambient coding agents that run for hours. For increasing probability of success, he emphasizes reliability through determinism: prototypes are easy but production is hard, and enterprises demand predictability and control. The solution is making more of the agent deterministic, blending workflows and agents rather than choosing one. LangGraph supports this spectrum, including multi-agent architectures. Observability and evaluation via LangSmith reduce stakeholder uncertainty, with a user reportedly gaining agent approval at a review panel and ending the meeting under time. For reducing cost when wrong, Chase recommends UI/UX patterns making agent actions easily reversible (Replit saving every file change as a commit) and human-in-the-loop patterns (opening PRs instead of direct merges). Deep research and Claude code exemplify this: upfront calibration questions increase alignment, and output is a draft for human review rather than direct action. Chase then extends the framework to ambient agents—event-triggered background agents enabling one-to-many scaling, unlimited concurrency, relaxed latency, and more complex multi-step operations. Crucially, ambient does not mean fully autonomous; human-in-the-loop patterns (approve/reject, edit tool calls, answer questions, time travel or human-on-the-loop) remain essential. Chase identifies an intermediate sync-to-async stage (exemplified by Factory's async coding agents) where humans kick off and calibrate agents that then run asynchronously. Agent inbox is proposed as a UX for surfacing actions needing approval. Email is highlighted as a natural ambient agent use case, with Chase sharing an open-source email agent. In Q&A, Chase explains code agents' funding success through verifiability (code and math enable training data bootstrapping) and the generalizable first-draft UX pattern applicable to legal and writing domains.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Agent success depends on three factors: value when right, probability of success, and cost when wrong, combined as (P(success) × value) − (cost when wrong) > running cost.
Higher-value agents come from targeting expensive verticals (legal, finance) and shifting to long-running autonomous agents rather than quick co-pilot answers.
Reliability is achieved by making more of the agent deterministic, blending workflows and agents; LangGraph supports this full spectrum.
Observability and evaluation (LangSmith) reduce stakeholder uncertainty and help agents gain production approval in enterprise review panels.
Cost when wrong is mitigated by reversibility (commits, PRs) and human-in-the-loop patterns that change the cost calculation in people's minds.

Ambient agents—event-triggered, running in the background—enable one-to-many scaling, unlimited concurrency, relaxed latency, and more complex operations, but still require human-in-the-loop oversight.
Ambient does not mean fully autonomous; approve/reject, edit, answer questions, and time-travel (human-on-the-loop) patterns keep humans engaged at key decision points.
Sync-to-async agents represent an intermediate stage between chat agents and fully ambient agents, where humans kick off and calibrate before the agent runs asynchronously.
Code agents succeed partly because code and math are verifiable domains enabling training data bootstrapping; the first-draft UX pattern generalizes to legal and writing.
Agent inbox is a proposed UX for surfacing agent actions requiring human approval, with email as a natural ambient agent use case.

sections.title: Introduction and three ingredients framework
sections.summary: Chase introduces the topic of reliable enterprise agents, credits Assaf (head of AI at Monday, GPT researcher author), and presents the three ingredients: value when right, probability of success, and cost when wrong. He frames an equation where P(success) × value minus cost when wrong must exceed running cost.

sections.title: Increasing value: high-value verticals and longer-running agents
sections.summary: To increase value, target high-value verticals (Harvey in legal, finance research/summarization) and shift UI/UX from quick answers toward deep research and ambient coding agents that run for hours, moving beyond co-pilots to autonomous background work.

sections.title: Increasing probability of success: determinism and LangGraph
sections.summary: Reliability is hard in production. Enterprises want predictability and control. The solution is making more of the agent deterministic, blending workflows and agents. LangGraph supports this spectrum, including multi-agent architectures that sit between pure workflow and pure agent.

sections.title: Observability and eval reduce stakeholder uncertainty
sections.summary: LangSmith provides observability and eval. Beyond developer use, it communicates agent internals to review panels and stakeholders, reducing uncertainty. A user got agent approval and ended the review meeting under time.

sections.title: Reducing cost when wrong: reversibility and human-in-the-loop
sections.summary: Enterprises have outsized fear of agents causing damage. Reversibility via commits (Replit) and human-in-the-loop patterns (PRs instead of direct merges) change cost calculations. Deep research and Claude code exemplify upfront calibration with humans, then producing drafts for review rather than taking direct action.

sections.title: Ambient agents: scaling through event-triggered background agents
sections.summary: Once an agent has positive expected value, scale it via ambient agents triggered by events rather than humans. This shifts from one-to-one chat to one-to-many, unlimited concurrency, relaxed latency requirements, and more complex multi-step operations. Crucially, ambient does not mean fully autonomous—human-in-the-loop patterns (approve/reject, edit tool calls, answer questions, time travel or human-on-the-loop) remain essential.

sections.title: Sync-to-async agents and agent inbox UX
sections.summary: Chase identifies an intermediate sync-to-async stage (Factory's async coding agents) between chat and ambient agents, where humans kick off and calibrate before the agent runs asynchronously. Agent inbox is proposed as a UX for surfacing actions needing approval. Email is highlighted as a natural ambient agent use case, with Chase sharing an open-source email agent via QR code.

sections.title: Q&A: Why code agents succeed—verifiability and first drafts
sections.summary: In Q&A, Chase explains code agents' funding success through two factors: verifiability of code and math enables training data bootstrapping making models better, and code lends itself to commit/draft/preview UX. The first-draft UX pattern generalizes to legal and writing domains, enabling agents to do substantial work while keeping humans in the loop at key points.

demonstrations: Replit agent screenshot showing diff/PR generation with each file change saved as a new commit for easy reversion
Deep research as example of human-in-the-loop: upfront calibration questions then producing a report for human review rather than direct action
Claude code asking clarifying questions and working on separate branches with PRs
Open-source email ambient agent built by Chase, with QR code linking to GitHub repo
limitations: Prototypes work once but production reliability is hard to achieve
Prompting an agent to always follow a step order may only work ~90% of the time, whereas deterministic code always works
There is outsized perception/fear of agents causing brand damage in enterprises
Verifiability of code and math domains is harder to generalize to ambiguous domains like essay writing
Human-in-the-loop at every step provides no value since each step is too small; the challenge is finding key intervention points
quantitativeClaims: Seven examples of ambient coding agents launched in the three weeks prior to the talk
A LangSmith user got agent approval at a review panel and ended the meeting under time
Ambient agents can scale from one concurrent agent (chat) to unlimited (event-triggered background agents)
